description: The Scaffy masterplan: scaffolding as commands — declarative, idempotent, reversible documents stored in Barkpark and executed by bp. Covers the lineage (PortableDoc for code), the .scaffy format and its mark mechanic, the verified Barkpark command catalog (add block-type flagship), add/remove symmetry, format-hardening findings, and the build roadmap.

tags.rationale: The design paper for Scaffy itself — commands as content.
Full architecture design: format, engine, catalog, roadmap.
States the propagation doctrine: runtime-collected, generated, or command-applied — never hand-maintained.
The engine lands as a bp subcommand in the Go CLI.

blocks.text: Commands as Content — the Scaffy Masterplan

content.value: Scaffy turns scaffolding into commands: declarative, idempotent, reversible documents that create files AND wire them into the registries, routers, barrels and index files a plain generator can never touch. Stored in Barkpark like Papers and Tasks, served over one connect, executed by bp — a command is a standard in runnable form. This paper is the full design: the lineage, the format, the mark mechanic, the Barkpark command catalog, and the add/remove symmetry that makes features portable.

blocks.text: The lineage — everything merges into Barkpark

content.value: Every organ of Barkpark followed the same move: take something the world treats as environment-bound, make it declarative and portable, then merge it in as a first-class content type. Scaffy applies that move to the last thing still bound to its repo: the code structure itself.

rows.value: one block truth, projected onto every surface
type:task documents on the same wire
a queryable x-ray of the codebase

content.value: Scaffy is PortableDoc for code.

blocks.caption: The loop: Cody perceives, truths constrain, Scaffy acts, features ship.
blocks.source:
flowchart LR
  C["Cody x-ray: patterns, dup, feature bounds"] --> T["Sources of truth: capabilities, schemas, tokens, canonical markers"]
  T --> S["Scaffy commands: create + inject + assert"]
  S --> F["Features: zip, transport, 1 connect"]
  F --> C

content.value: A generator stamps files once and walks away. A command is a maintained artifact that owns a repeated shape end to end: it creates the vertical slice, injects the wiring at guarded anchors, proves the result with assertions, and can retract everything it added. Run it twice — nothing happens. Run it with new variables — the new instance lands beside the old one, at markers the first run planted.

items.value: VARIABLES with prompts, examples and case morphology (singular + plural)
CREATE FILE IF ABSENT — the owned files of the slice
IN … INSERT/REPLACE … guarded — the connective tissue: index files, registries, routers
MARK — planted anchors that make re-runs, sibling runs and removal deterministic
ASSERT — postconditions that run the project's own gates
goals + hints — the agent-readable layer for when anchors drift

content.value: A documented standard describes; a linter punishes after the fact. A command IS the standard, executable. Nobody deviates because deviating is slower than conforming — the paved road wins every time, and when the standard changes you change one command.

blocks.title: Why this beats docs and linters

content.value: A standard that isn't executable is a wish.
Commands are authored in a sentence-shaped DSL (or in a GUI, stored as structured content — same artifact, two faces). The header carries catalog taxonomy; every op reads as English.

blocks.value:
COMMAND "Add PortableDoc Block Type"
DESCRIPTION "New block rendered on all four surfaces from commit one."
DOMAIN "barkpark" CONCEPT "block-type" VARIANT "leaf"
VARIABLES
  VARIABLE 1 "BlockName" TITLE "Block type name"
    EXAMPLES "timeline", "gantt", "poll"

content.value: Variable tokens carry their transform in their own spelling — write the token in the case you want out, and canonicalization folds every spelling back to one prompt:

The hardest problem in code injection is anchor fragility: anchoring on live code lines breaks the moment someone refactors. Marks solve it — the first run anchors on a structural target and plants a marker comment; every later run anchors on the mark.

blocks.value:
IN "internal/pdrender/pdrender.go"
### Register renderer in DefaultRegistry
INSERT
::: payload :::
	r.blocks["{{.block-name}}"] = {{.blockName}}Renderer{ir: ir}
::: payload :::
BELOW FIRST "r.blocks[\"PdSheet\"]"     # structural target, first run only
MARK "SCAFFY BLOCK REGISTRY"            # planted; primary anchor forever after

content.value: Run 1 (timeline) plants the mark. Run 2 (gantt) lands at the mark, beside its sibling. The command converts the host file into a registry as a side effect — and the mark is the retraction handle for remove.

blocks.title: Marks make commands accretive, not just idempotent

content.value: Adding a PortableDoc block type is Barkpark's four-surface parity monster: a Go renderer in the TUI, an Elixir clause in the reader, a JS emitter in the SDK, and edit CSS in Studio. Today that shape is held together by parity sweeps and audits after the fact. One command makes parity a birth property.

blocks.value:
barkpark/                                   # ● created   ○ injected
├── internal/pdrender/
│   ├── timeline.go                         # ● renderer
│   ├── timeline_test.go                    # ● golden test
│   └── pdrender.go                         # ○ r.blocks["timeline"] = …
├── api/lib/barkpark/portable_doc/
│   └── render.ex                           # ○ render clause (render_block/2)
├── js/packages/react/src/blocks/
│   ├── timeline.ts                         # ● emitter
│   └── registry.ts                         # ○ registration line
└── api/lib/barkpark_web/components/layouts/
    └── root.html.heex                      # ○ .bp-timeline edit CSS

content.value: Two files created, four registries injected — each at a marked anchor, each guarded, and the run ends by proving the wiring:

blocks.value:
ASSERT FILE "internal/pdrender/pdrender.go"            CONTAINS "r.blocks[\"{{.block-name}}\"]"
ASSERT FILE "js/packages/react/src/blocks/registry.ts" CONTAINS "{{.block-name}}"
ASSERT CMD  "go test ./internal/pdrender/ -run {{.BlockName}}" EXIT 0

content.value: $ bp add block-type --var BlockName=timeline
created   internal/pdrender/timeline.go
created   internal/pdrender/timeline_test.go
created   js/packages/react/src/blocks/timeline.ts
inserted  4 registrations (marks planted)
asserts   3/3 pass — parity at birth
$ bp add block-type --var BlockName=timeline
0 created, 0 inserted, 7 skipped (already present)

blocks.footer: idempotent · re-run is a no-op · remove retracts the marks

content.value: Ranked by frequency times pain — how often we give birth to the shape, times how much of it is tribal knowledge today. Anchors verified against the live tree.

rows.value: canonical minimal callback set is tribal knowledge
the layer-parity sweep, as construction instead of detection
7-card cap forces the remove path — symmetry proof
one INSERT; manifest does the rest
the 'grep whole lib/ + test/' warning, encoded

content.value: Barkpark already beat accretion inside the BEAM: the plugin behaviour collects routes, crontabs, schemas and CLI verbs at runtime, and the bp binary derives its whole surface from the capabilities manifest. Never write-time-template what a runtime collector or generator already derives. Commands are the third propagation mechanism, for the residue the other two cannot reach — everything cross-runtime.

rows.value: cross-runtime residue: Go, JS, CSS, config, docs

content.value: Remove is the half everyone skips, and it is what turns a scaffolder into architecture. If everything a command adds is attributable — whole owned files, mark-bounded insertions — then removal is mechanical: delete the owned files, retract the marked spans, replay the apply receipt in reverse. That constraint forbids entangled contributions and forces every feature to stay a clean vertical slice.

blocks.value:
tickets.feature.zip
├── files/                        # the whole slice, all runtimes
│   ├── api/…/plugins/tickets/    #   Elixir plugin
│   ├── internal/…                #   Go CLI/TUI parts
│   └── js/…                      #   SDK parts
└── feature.scaffy                # the connective tissue, declared:
                                  #   every registry line, marked + guarded

content.value: Unzip anywhere Barkpark-shaped, run, one connect — the feature wires itself in. Guards make its footprint detectable, hence removable, hence swappable. The repo becomes a socket board; features become plugs.

Without marks and receipts, insertions are orphans the day they land — unremovable, unattributable, invisible to the next command. Every mutating op must plant its mark. This is the difference between scaffolding a repo and littering it.

A close review of the reference command (698 lines, the page-type scaffold) found the voice right and the guarantees missing. Three real bugs were sitting in the example — each preventable at validate time.

rows.value: fence anchors and targets like payloads
Hand-typed guards drift from their own payloads (re-insert loop found)
derive guards from the rendered payload by default; validate overrides
'CONTAIN START AND END OF TARGET' is unspecified magic
explicit REPLACE FROM … TO … WITH grammar
No mark planting → no remove, no sibling accretion
strict mode: every token must resolve to a declared VARIABLE
Casing divergence between path and URL tokens (404 found)
lint: same variable, path vs URL casing must agree
Import management via weak textual guard (dead op found)

items.value: Harden the format: fenced anchors, derived guards, MARK + receipts, strict tokens, SNIPPET.
Engine: Scaffy's Go core (parser, executor, guards, marks, asserts) as a bp subcommand — same binary, manifest-driven.
Command as a Barkpark document type: authored in Studio or as .scaffy, stored, versioned, tagged, served.
Flagship: add block-type — highest run count ahead (11 wanted data-viz blocks), worst manual cost, cleanest anchors.
Second: add docs-card + remove docs-card — the 7-card cap forces symmetry immediately, pure-markdown risk.
Catalog: one command per 'typical thing', concept × variant, browsable in the dashboard, installable via bp.

content.value: The catalog is no longer hypothetical: the full Wave-1 command corpus — every .scaffy file at full text, with run and re-run transcripts — is on display in
Scaffy in Action: the Command Showcase
at /papers/scaffy-command-showcase.

Commands are served now. The Wave-4 loop this paper argued for is live: the seven commands above exist as command documents on the connected Barkpark, served over one connect exactly like Papers and Tasks —
bp scaffy ls --remote
renders the server's catalog, and any command is pulled from a connected Barkpark via
bp scaffy pull <concept>/<variant>

— validated before anything can run, written byte-identical (sha256-verified against the served source) beside a provenance sidecar. Remote content stays inside the trust model: pull never executes, and running a pulled command is consent-gated — without an explicit --yes it refuses with the full list of substituted CMDs it would run — see the showcase.

Every fact has one owner; every derived surface is collected at runtime, generated from a manifest, or applied by a command — and never maintained by hand. Cody sees, truths constrain, Scaffy acts. Fast scaffolding is the forcing function that keeps the codebase standard-shaped.
